title: Agent systems are provenance-blind when skills are treated as tool calls
content:
## Claim

When skill invocations are recorded only as tool calls and log lines, the downstream artifact carries no structured trace of which skill produced which fragment under whose authority.

## Why it matters

Without that trace, evaluation collapses to output scoring, safety auditing has only the prompt and final string to inspect, and knowledge claims become unfalsifiable—even a true answer cannot be shown to come from a reliable process.

## Evidence from source

The paper frames this as the missing fourth question in the Agent Skills literature: not only how to design, evaluate, and secure skills, but how to *record what a skill did*.

## Methodology grounding
The claims below live in the plugin's `data/methodology/` corpus; the relationship is stated per claim.

- **[[agents are simultaneously methodology executors and subjects creating a unique trust asymmetry]]** — BUILDS_ON. Provenance blindness is obliviousness seen from the outside: the methodology claim borrows Kiczales' term for base code that cannot observe the aspects modifying it, and a tool call is exactly a transformation whose provenance the calling agent cannot see.
- **[[prospective memory requires externalization]]** — RELATES_TO. A tool call leaves nothing for a later session to read, so any obligation it created is lost at the session boundary — the failure mode that claim generalises.
description: Tool-call logs record arguments and returns but not which skill wrote which artifact fragment, so evaluation and audit collapse.
